newsitem.title: INDIA: Chidambaram gathers input for India Companies Bill.
newsitem.headline: Chidambaram gathers input for India Companies Bill.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P.Chidambaram on Friday sought ideas on framing a Companies Bill which he hopes will be implemented in April 1998.
"I consider (this) the most important item on the agenda regarding the corporate sector," Chidambaram told a seminar organised by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
The heart of the bill will be legislation dealing with disclosure and governance, he said.
Chidambaram emphasised the need to develop a code of conduct and ethics in a country beset by scandals in business and politics.
He said India needed the judicial "machinery that will punish bad professional conduct and behaviour swiftly and severely."

A working draft of the bill was opened for discussion among business people, lawyers and judges in order to hone a final draft to be presented during the monsoon session of parliament opening July 23.
Chidambaram said he hoped it would be passed by the end of the year.
"If all goes well we will have a brand new company law effective from April 1, 1998," the minister said.
He served warning to corporate groups to keep the affairs of their companies in order.
"Groups bring synergy. A group can also be an exploitative cover for a number of misdeeds," he said.
India's financial community and its regulators are currently reeling from the collapse of the CRB group of companies, a non-bank finance group which has failed.
He listed the need to decide appropriate debt/equity levels following share buy backs, and to identify what category of companies should be allowed to raise deposits from the public.
He also said nepotism had no place in a corporate sector which requires strong, professional management.
The bill also had to determine the level of disclosure required from companies, putting norms in place whereby companies can practice self-regulation.
If business failed to pratice adequate self-regulation he warned external regulations will become "harsher and harsher and quite indiscriminate."

"The heart of the compnay law is disclosure and governance. I would urge you to look at the disclosure norms and make it as comprehensive as possible so that self regulation is the primary regulation, and external regulation is merely a check on self regulation," he said.
